module_title: Condonation of Delay, Legal Disability, and Continuous Time
introduction: This intermediate tier explores the strict exceptions under the Act. It details when the court can forgive a delay (Section 5), how minors and insane persons are protected (Section 6), and the relentless nature of time once it begins to run (Section 9).

core_concepts.title: Condonation of Delay (Section 5)
core_concepts.description:
When the court forgives you for being late.
- The Rule: Any **appeal or application** may be admitted after the prescribed period if the appellant or applicant satisfies the court that he had **'sufficient cause'** for not preferring the appeal or making the application within such period (e.g., severe illness, imprisonment).
- The Ultimate Trap: Section 5 **DOES NOT APPLY TO SUITS**. You can NEVER file an original civil lawsuit late and ask for forgiveness claiming 'sufficient cause'. The court has zero power to extend the limitation for a suit.

core_concepts.title: Legal Disability (Sections 6, 7 & 8)
core_concepts.description:
Protection for vulnerable individuals.
- The Rule (Sec 6): If a person is a **Minor**, **Insane**, or an **Idiot** at the time the cause of action arises, the limitation period does NOT start running against them. It only starts running after their disability ceases (e.g., the minor turns 18).
- Double Disability: If a person is affected by two disabilities (e.g., a minor who is also insane), time does not run until BOTH disabilities end.
- Section 8 Cap: Once the disability ceases, the person gets an extension of the limitation period, but this extension can **NEVER exceed 3 years** from the date the disability ended.

core_concepts.title: Continuous Running of Time (Section 9)
core_concepts.description:
The unstoppable clock rule.
- The Rule: 'Where once time has begun to run, no subsequent disability or inability to institute a suit or make an application stops it.'
- Application: If A has a right to sue B (limitation 3 years). After 1 year of the time running, A goes completely insane. Does the clock pause? **NO**. Because A was sane when the cause of action *arose*, the clock started. A subsequent/later disability cannot stop the relentless march of limitation.

core_concepts.title: Exclusion of Time in Legal Proceedings (Section 12 & 14)
core_concepts.description:
- Section 12: In computing the period of limitation, the day from which the period is to be reckoned is excluded. Also, the time required to obtain a copy of the decree/judgment is excluded when filing an appeal.
- Section 14: If a plaintiff prosecuted a case in good faith and with due diligence in a court that ultimately had **no jurisdiction** to hear it, the time spent fighting in that wrong court is completely excluded when calculating limitation for the correct court.

important_entities.name: Sufficient Cause
important_entities.significance: The Supreme Court (*Collector, Land Acquisition v. Katiji*) has ruled that 'sufficient cause' should receive a liberal construction to advance substantial justice. However, mere negligence or inaction is not a sufficient cause.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.alert_title: The 'Section 5 applies to Suits' Fatal Trap
trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: This is the most frequent trick question in CLAT PG and Judiciary exams. A scenario will describe a poor, illiterate farmer who missed the 3-year deadline to file a *Suit* by 2 days because he was in a coma. The examiner asks: 'Can the court condone the delay under Section 5?' **ABSOLUTELY NOT**. Section 5 explicitly excludes original suits. The suit must be dismissed under Section 3.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: These are the ONLY three legal disabilities recognized by Section 6 of the Limitation Act. Illiteracy, poverty, or imprisonment are NOT legal disabilities.

exam_strategy_tips: If an exam asks 'What is the maximum period of extension allowed after the cessation of a legal disability under Section 8?', unconditionally select **3 years**.
